Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
ruminate about how event could have been prevented
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

issues.explanation: These items form a combat/interpersonal-violence style hypervigilance pattern centered on armed human threat, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma. A disaster survivor may be generally vigilant, but carrying a weapon and scanning for weapons specifically are not a coherent extension of the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: The threat profile is narrowly organized around deliberate human attack (weapons, tactical positioning), while the memory items are generic intrusion/detachment phenomena and do not support that specific threat theme. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a plausible disaster-related PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Gerald is a 74-year-old man of German descent who lives with his long-term partner in a mid-sized town in the Pacific Northwest, where he works part-time as a private tutor, helping high school students with mathematics and history. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 48, seeking help approximately fourteen months after surviving a severe wildfire that swept through the rural edge of his community during a dry August.

Gerald had been at home when the fire crested the ridge faster than any forecast had predicted. The air turned brown, then orange, and the smell - a dense, resinous burning that seemed to coat the inside of his lungs - arrived before the flames were visible. He spent nearly two hours sheltering in his car in a parking lot, watching the horizon pulse with light, uncertain whether emergency services knew where he was, uncertain whether his partner, who had been out running errands, was safe. It was the waiting, the helplessness inside that car, the acrid smell seeping through the vents, that seemed to lodge itself most deeply in him. When his partner finally appeared through the smoke-hazed lot, Gerald wept with a relief he could not afterward explain without returning, involuntarily, to those two hours.

In the months that followed, the memory began to behave in ways Gerald found deeply unsettling. It did not wait for him to choose to revisit it. During tutoring sessions - quiet afternoons at his kitchen table with a teenager working through algebra - the memory would force itself forward without warning, arriving not as a recollection he had sought but as an interruption he could not refuse. More disturbing still, the smell would sometimes accompany it: that same thick, resinous burning, arriving in a room where there was nothing burning at all. These intrusions left him shaken and searching for ways to manage what he could not stop. He had begun telling himself, with increasing deliberateness, that the fire had really happened to someone else - a kind of mental stepping-back, a pretence of distance that allowed him to function through a session without visibly falling apart. He also found himself spending long stretches of time turning the event over in his mind, rehearsing the sequence of decisions made that morning, trying to identify the precise moment at which things might have gone differently - as if the right answer, found late enough, might retroactively make him safer.

These strategies, however, did not quiet the memory. If anything, the rumination kept the event close, and the dissociative pretence seemed only to preserve its strangeness - when the memory did break through, it sometimes arrived in that flattened, affectless register, as though it had happened to a stranger, which frightened Gerald in its own way. The memory's intrusive quality fed directly into how he now read his environment: he had become convinced that danger was always proximate and that his own perception was the only reliable early-warning system. During tutoring sessions, he now insisted on sitting with his back to the wall, positioned so he could see both the door and the window simultaneously. When a student's parent was late to collect a child, Gerald's chest would tighten with the certainty that something had gone wrong - an accident, another emergency, something unfolding outside that he could not yet see. He scanned constantly: the quality of light through the window, the smell of the air, the distant sound of sirens.

This vigilance in turn reinforced the strategies that had initially seemed protective. Because he was always monitoring, always braced, the effort of getting through a tutoring afternoon had become exhausting, and he had begun declining any engagement he judged potentially stressful - social invitations, driving routes that passed near forested hillsides, any situation in which he could not control his position in a room. His partner had noticed the narrowing. Gerald had noticed it too.

What finally brought him to seek help was a session in which a student asked, offhandedly, whether Gerald could smell smoke. There was no smoke. Gerald had excused himself, gone to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink for several minutes. He came to the first appointment hoping, above everything else, to stop being afraid of his own mind.
